Description: The PhD in Disability Studies at the University of Illinois Chicago is an interdisciplinary program that views disability as a complex relationship between society and individuals who differ from the norm. [2] The program's goal is to foster an understanding of disability that empowers individuals in forming their identities and lives, while also examining how support services and societal and political changes can mitigate sources of disempowerment. [2] It is designed as a full-time course of study, and students will have an advisor from the program faculty to guide their progress. [3] The curriculum is interdisciplinary, with faculty and students from diverse fields such as health, education, assistive technology, social sciences, and humanities. [2] Students will develop advanced knowledge of the complex social implications of disability and acquire skills in research leadership, policy analysis, and program evaluation. [2] A dissertation is required for the completion of the degree. [3]

Description: The MSE doctoral program spans P-20 mathematics and science education in urban settings in and out of schools. [1] The focus is on developing new knowledge that improves science and mathematics education and has an impact on the communities we serve. [1] Students engage in coursework and research experiences that guide them to view issues of learning, teaching, curriculum, assessment, and policy through sociocultural and sociopolitical lenses where equity, social justice, race, language, culture, and identity are essential considerations. [1] Students who enroll in the MSE PhD program are required to complete a minimum of 98 semester hours of coursework beyond the baccalaureate degree or 66 hours beyond the Master's degree. [1] Coursework beyond the Master's includes 24 hours of the College of Education core, 12 hours of the MSE core, and 12 hours in one of the two disciplinary strands (i.e., mathematics education or science education). [1] Program faculty members are widely recognized as leaders in their respective fields. [1] They have published extensively on the educational experiences of African American and Latino learners, and bring to their research and teaching strong disciplinary education in STEM fields. [1] They also have considerable records of mentoring and preparing scholars from traditionally underrepresented groups, as well as preparing and collaborating with P-20 science and mathematics teachers and faculty. [1] Graduates of the MSE program are well-prepared to assume a variety of positions in colleges, universities and informal educational settings to improve the mathematics and science education for children, adolescents and adult learners through research. [1]

Graduates become research experts and innovators in one of two focus areas; Human Development and Learning or Measurement, Evaluation, Statistics, and Assessment. Nevertheless, all graduates are expected to have knowledge of the main areas of research found in the field of Educational Psychology.

Description: The PhD in English at the University of Illinois Chicago requires a minimum of 96 semester hours from the baccalaureate or 76 from the MA. Students are not given credit for courses with a grade lower than B. The program offers specializations in English Studies, English Education, and Creative Writing (also known as the Program for Writers). Students in English Studies or English Education design their program with a faculty advisor, while those in Creative Writing have specific workshop requirements. For instance, fiction, poetry, and nonfiction writers must each take at least 8 hours in their respective workshops. The program also requires a preliminary examination, a prospectus, and a dissertation (32 hours of ENGL 599). Additionally, students must take ENGL 555 in preparation for teaching assistantships. [9, 5]

Description: The Department of Germanic Studies is a vibrant intellectual community of scholars and students with a broad range of interests. Housed in the School of Literatures, Cultural Studies, and Linguistics, our department is particularly attuned to the linkages between German culture, transnational identities, and urban spaces. We actively foster dialogues with the diverse cultural and social groups represented in the university and in the greater Chicago area. Graduate students can gain interdepartmental concentrations in Black Studies, Central and Eastern European Studies, Gender and Women's Studies, and Jewish Studies, and they can study in Berlin through our exchange program with the Humboldt University.

Description: Die Abteilung für medizinische Ausbildung (DME) freut sich, die Einrichtung eines neuen Online-PhD-Programms in Health Professions Education (HPE) bekannt zu geben. Der PhD in HPE ist aus unserer erfolgreichen früheren Zusammenarbeit mit der Abteilung für Lehrplan und Unterricht des UIC College of Education hervorgegangen. Der PhD in HPE baut auch auf dem Erfolg und dem guten Ruf des Master of Health Professions Education (MHPE) der DME sowie auf der breiteren Expertise der Abteilung in der HPE-Forschung und der hervorragenden Lehre auf. Das PhD in HPE-Programm wird exemplarische Wissenschaftler hervorbringen, die das Gebiet der Ausbildung in den Gesundheitsberufen voranbringen, indem sie innovative Forschungsagenden entwickeln, die die Bildungspolitik, -standards und -praktiken gestalten, mit dem letztendlichen Ziel, die Gesundheitsversorgung zu verbessern. Obwohl das PhD-Programm in HPE Kursangebote mit dem renommierten MHPE-Programm von DME teilen wird, wird es einen größeren Schwerpunkt auf Forschungsdesign, Datenerfassung und originelle wissenschaftliche Arbeit für Studenten legen, die in Zukunft als leitende Forscher in HPE-Studien fungieren möchten.

ProgramName: PhD in Industrial Engineering and Operations Research
Department: College of Engineering
Description: The PhD in Industrial Engineering and Operations Research helps students develop expertise in core disciplines in industrial engineering, such as data-driven decision-making and design, controls, and manufacturing. [6] The PhD requires 108 semester hours of credit from the baccalaureate, beginning with coursework and culminating in the research, writing, and defense of an original dissertation. [6, 5] Students develop their own research agendas in one (or more) of the department's research labs, working with faculty mentors. [8] The program welcomes applicants with a relevant master's degree as well as applicants with only an undergraduate degree. [6]

Description: The PhD in Pharmacy is a highly competitive, STEM-designated graduate program that attracts students from all over the world. Housed in the UIC Department of Pharmacy Systems, Outcomes and Policy (PSOP), the PhD program is supported by PSOP faculty and staff who are dedicated to the education of future pharmacists and pharmacy researchers. [2] The program provides intensive coursework and strong emphasis is placed on combining fundamentals of statistics and research design with theoretical frameworks from decision and information sciences, economics, psychology, epidemiology, communication, public health, and education. [2] With today's emphasis on both the cost and quality of health care, opportunities abound for those with research expertise in pharmacy systems, outcomes, and policy. [2] Employers from the pharmaceutical industry, consulting organizations, government agencies, managed care companies, academia, and others are highly interested in individuals who can integrate and apply knowledge in biostatistics and research design with social sciences in order to study pharmacy services, pharmaceutical products, patient and health system outcomes, and pharmaceutical and health policy. Description: The UIC Graduate Program in Philosophy is a Ph.D. program. Most of our faculty were trained in analytic philosophy, and their research and teaching interests reflect that basic orientation. [4] Admitted students proceed toward the Ph.D. in two stages. The first stage centers around graduate seminars and, later, special preparation in the area of the doctoral dissertation. This stage typically takes three years. During the first two and a half years, the student takes at least 14 regularly scheduled graduate courses, mostly seminars, at the rate of 3 per semester. [4] These must be chosen so that the student satisfies course requirements in logic (one course), history of philosophy (three courses with at least one in ancient or medieval and at least one in modern philosophy), and three distribution areas — metaphysics or epistemology; philosophy of language, philosophy of science, or philosophy of logic; and ethics, social and political philosophy, aesthetics, or philosophy of law — (five courses with at least one in each of the three areas). [4] The second stage is expected to take two years, making the Ph.D. program a five-year program. [4]

[5] Students will have the opportunity to engage in critical, activist scholarship on diversity, equity and social justice in education. [5] The PhD concentration in Educational Leadership & Policy (ELP) is specifically dedicated to the study of policy creation and implementation in urban educational contexts, the role of leadership in promoting equity and improving schools, and the study of school leader preparation for urban schools. [6] This PhD concentration supports students' research from a range of perspectives, including policy formation and implementation, organizational and leadership theories, and improving equity in schools. [6]

Individuals with master's degrees in related disciplines (for example, psychology or sociology) may choose to earn a PhD in Social Work without first earning the MSW. Credit from a related master's degree may be applied to the PhD degree program, as determined by the School of Social Work. Students complete required coursework, research, and teaching practicums; pass a comprehensive exam; write a dissertation; and defend the dissertation in an oral exam. Their work includes courses in one of four outside disciplines—sociology, psychology, public health, or education—to assist them in preparation for the comprehensive examination and dissertation. Department: School of Architecture
Description: The Master of Arts in Design Criticism (MAD-Crit) is a two-year program thatdevelops textual and visual argumentation in the areas of architecture,urbanism, landscape, and allied design practices. With the seemingly limitlessexpansion of design techniques and productive capacities today, there exists anew urgency for a parallel polemics that can contribute the conceptualarmature and directives for the immediate future of design culture. Revolvingaround intensive writing seminars and publication workshops, the ambition of theprogram is unabashedly operative: i.e., it is driven by the practice of writingand the demand to inject argument immediately into diverse media ofcommunication. This operative orientation is accelerated by being situatedwithin a School of Architecture focused on contemporary design, and through theprogram's overlapping coursework with the MArch and MS programs, such asparticipation in its research studios and publications. Today, architecture andits corollary design fields have become increasingly compelled toward academicand professional specialization. While producing important scholarly andtechnical advances, this context has undermined if not obliterated thepotential role for those invested in design culture as public intellectual. TheMAD-Crit program aims to recover this generalist role that has been lost in theproliferation of doctoral programs and software niches. Taking advantage ofits location in a major American metropolis and at public research university,the MAD-Crit program is particularly well-situated to solicit and expand theaudience for design criticism and reposition the significance of design inpublic discourse. Moreover, as the product of design competitions areincreasingly gravitating to books and arguments, the program understandscriticism broadly to include proactive design propositions. At UIC, criticism serves as an invitation for new practices rather than a retrospective callingout of existing ones; it is a platform for future production. The MAD-Critprogram is committed to empowering a new generation of idea activists for thediscipline.

Department: College of Engineering and College of Architecture, Design, and the Arts (School of Design)

ProgramName: BA in Criminology, Law, and Justice
Requirements: While the official University of Illinois at Chicago (UIC) website does not provide a specific set of application requirements for the 'BA in Criminology, Law, and Justice' program itself, admission to undergraduate programs is handled at a university level. Prospective students must meet the general first-year admission requirements of UIC. These general requirements are not detailed on the Criminology, Law, and Justice program page.
Description: Criminology is the scientific study of crime and criminal behavior. Knowledge gained from the scientific study of crime and criminal justice serves as the foundation for public policies and programs that improve the quality of life and promote social justice. Criminal Justice is concerned with the study of all aspects of crime and societal reactions to crime. Examining political, economic, and cultural patterns that shape definitions of crime and influence the policy choices about how to respond to certain criminal and deviant behaviors is central to this discipline. With a BA in Criminology, Law, and Justice, you will recognize the causes and consequences of crime at the micro and macro levels and be able to match these with prominent criminological perspectives. [1] You will understand the interrelated institutions and processes of the criminal justice system and legal systems. [1]

ProgramName: Minor in Criminology, Law, and Justice

Description: Students from other disciplines who want to minor in Criminology, Law, and Justice must complete 18 semester hours as outlined below: Required Courses CLJ 101 Introduction to Criminology, Law, and Justice 3 CLJ 200 Law and Society 3 CLJ 210 Principles of Criminal Law 3 CLJ 220 Criminology 3 Two courses at the 300 or 400 level chosen with the consent of the advisor. 6 Total Hours 18.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Disability and Human Development
Requirements: General application requirements vary between undergraduate and graduate admissions. For graduate applicants, a bachelor's degree from an accredited institution with a minimum GPA of 3.0/4.0 is generally required, though specific programs may have higher standards. For undergraduate (freshman) applicants, admission is test-optional, meaning ACT/SAT scores are not required. The review process is holistic, considering academic performance, the rigor of high school coursework, and supplemental materials.
Department: College of Applied Health Sciences
Description: Our Bachelor of Science in Disability and Human Development (DHD) explores disability as a complex biological, social, cultural, political, historical and economic experience. [1] DHD students learn about strategies to remove barriers to people with disabilities. [1] They learn to think critically about how to reshape society and the built environment in a more just way. [1] We are committed to universally-designed instruction, providing barrier-free learning environments where all students can thrive. [1] The Department of Disability and Human Development mobilizes its relationships with community partners and disability organizations as well as its leadership within the fields of disability and human development and disability studies to provide students with a broad, interdisciplinary degree that blends theory, research, and practice. [2]

ProgramName: Minor in Disability and Human Development
Requirements: The Minor in Disability Inclusion is open to majors in the College of Applied Health Sciences and from other units and colleges. [2] To apply, students must have a minimum UIC GPA of 2.5 on a 4.0 scale and submit an online application form. [3] Applicants should also consult their home college regarding the acceptability and applicability of DHD course credit toward their degree. [3]
Department: College of Applied Health Sciences, Department of Disability and Human Development
Description: The minor in Disability and Human Development offers an interdisciplinary study of disability, focusing on overarching issues of inclusion for people with disabilities in areas of policy, technology, community, arts, culture, and health. The minor is being renamed from “Disability and Human Development” to “Disability Inclusion” to more accurately reflect the identity of the program and advances in the field. [3]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Earth and Environmental Sciences
Requirements: The University of Illinois at Chicago (UIC) does not offer a 'Bachelor of Arts in Earth and Environmental Sciences' but does offer a Bachelor of Science (BS) in the field. The application requirements for this program fall under the general first-year admission standards. Prospective students must complete the Common Application, including any UIC-specific questions and essays. [2] A nonrefundable application fee (or a fee waiver) and official high school transcripts are also required for the application to be complete. [2]
Department: College of Liberal Arts and Sciences
Description: The University of Illinois at Chicago website lists a Bachelor of Science (BS) in Earth and Environmental Sciences, but not a Bachelor of Arts (BA) in Earth and Environmental Sciences. The Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences offers a Bachelor of Science (BS), Master of Science (MS), and Doctor of Philosophy (PhD), as well as a minor. [8] The BS program is designed to help students explore and study the natural world, including topics like climate change, urban pollution, and planetary formation. [9] It prepares students for employment and post-graduate work in geoscience and environmental science. [9] The curriculum provides broad training in interdisciplinary earth science and involves research through fieldwork, laboratory investigations, and computational modeling. [8] Earth is studied as a dynamic body, and understanding its system processes is key to evaluating the global environment and changes resulting from human activity. [11]

ProgramName: Minor in Earth and Environmental Sciences
Requirements: To declare a minor in Earth and Environmental Sciences, students must complete 18 semester hours in EAES coursework, which must be chosen with the approval of the department. A minimum of 9 hours must be at the 200 level or above, and students are required to take either EAES 300 or EAES 302. [3]

First-year applicants must submit the Common Application, a nonrefundable application fee, and official high school transcripts. [11, 25] Submission of ACT or SAT scores is optional. [11] Graduate admission requirements vary by program but generally include an online application and transcripts from all previous schools. [7, 15] International applicants may have additional requirements, including proof of English proficiency. [12]

[7] Applicants apply via the Common Application. [3]

To declare a minor in Economics, a student must be a current UIC student. The minor requires the completion of 18-20 semester hours. The required courses include ECON 120 (Principles of Microeconomics), ECON 121 (Principles of Macroeconomics), and either ECON 220 (Microeconomics: Theory and Applications) or ECON 221 (Macroeconomics in the World Economy: Theory and Applications). Additionally, students must complete three economics courses at the 200, 300, or 400 level.
Description: Students who wish to take some economics coursework may consider our Minor in Economics, which requires six courses. The minor is often a good complement to majors in finance, business, political science, sociology, mathematics, premed, engineering, and other related fields. [8]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering
Department: Department of Electrical Engineering
Concentration: ['Analog and Mixed-Signal Circuits', 'Communications', 'Computer and Networked Systems', 'Control, Robotics, and Embedded Systems', 'Data Science and Engineering', 'Digital Systems and VLSI', 'Electromagnetics']
Description: The Electrical Engineering curriculum is concerned with analysis and design of modern electronic systems, devices, and signals for a broad range of applications such as wireless or network communication, electrical power and control, and multimedia information technology. [4] The curriculum provides a wide background in the fundamental theory of electrical engineering and in the mathematical and scientific tools necessary for an electrical engineer to meet the current and future challenges of a professional career. [4] The field of electrical engineering is currently evolving at a rapid pace since it has a major role in the accelerated growth of the technological world. [4] This requires the modern electrical engineer not only to have a sound basis in the fundamental principles but also to have the capacity to learn and assimilate novel advances as soon as they materialize. [4] These qualities are anticipated in the curriculum, which includes not only a sound theoretical background but also offers a variety of courses that develop the student's ability to gain knowledge autonomously and to combine it with contemporary design techniques. [4] Courses are in diverse areas such as signal processing, power electronics, communications, optical and electromagnetic technologies, control systems, integrated circuits, multimedia networks, and image analysis. [4] The curriculum includes both required and elective courses. [4] The required courses are in engineering, mathematics, and physics; they provide a wide backdrop in science and engineering. The elective courses are more specialized and offer a broad range of electrical engineering applications. [4]
Accredidation: The electrical engineering program at UIC is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET. [4, 5]

Description: The Bachelor of Science in Finance program at UIC provides students with a comprehensive understanding of financial principles and practices. It is designed to be an experiential program, combining the expertise of top faculty, a robust curriculum with multiple concentration options, industry support, and various student organizations and initiatives. The curriculum is structured to assist students in pursuing their desired careers in finance, with a wide array of elective courses covering areas such as corporate financial analysis, business valuation, investments and portfolio management, banking, international finance, trading, and risk management. The program leverages its close connections to Chicago's financial markets to offer valuable experiential learning opportunities. Students will gain both theoretical knowledge and practical skills in a stimulating and active learning environment, preparing them to be strategic decision-makers who can analyze financial statements, forecast financial performance, and make informed recommendations on investments and business operations.

Modern finance is remarkably diverse, drawing from many disciplines beyond economics, including mathematics, statistics, operations research, engineering, computer science, psychology, and politics. In addition to the obvious practical relevance of finance, the field contains both challenging intellectual problems and a distinctive conceptual framework. With a Minor in Finance, students enhance their resumes and strengthen their applications for graduate school and many competitive job markets.

All intermediate and advanced courses help students achieve two interlocking goals. First, all courses foster proficiency in speaking, reading, and writing French, as well as understanding how the language is woven into diverse cultural contexts in Francophone countries throughout the world. Second, all courses help students develop a historical sense of French-speaking cultures, as well as the critical and interpretive skills that come from analytical reading, active discussion, and persuasive writing. A major or a minor in French and Francophone Studies gives students a strong, globally oriented foundation for careers in many fields, such as education, international commerce, law, government, and journalism.

[7] Academic inquiry into the changing roles of women and men, gay, lesbian, bisexual, queer, and transgender people allows students to understand themselves and their relationships with others and helps them make informed choices about their own lives. ProgramName: Bachelor of Arts in Germanic Studies

Description: The department offers programs leading to the Bachelor of Arts with a Major in Germanic Studies and the BA in the Teaching of German. A minor is offered in the Germanic Studies as well. The Department of Germanic Studies offers language and culture courses at the beginning, intermediate, and advanced levels. Courses at all levels emphasize the development of language fluency and cultural competency, as well as critical-thinking and effective writing skills. Course offerings cover a wide array of topics including film, Business German, and contemporary media. Courses in Yiddish language, literature, and culture are also offered. Students who major or minor in Germanic Studies may use their training in a variety of occupations, including teaching, translation, international marketing, banking and commerce, diplomatic service, and journalism. [5]

Department: College of Liberal Arts and Sciences
Description: Global Asian Studies a an Interdisciplinary study of Asia, as well as transoceanic and transnational Asian diasporas. [5] While emphasizing the study of Asian and Asian American geographies, histories, languages, cultures, and politics, GLAS scrutinizes the frames of area studies and ethnic studies within which such analyses have traditionally been located. [5] With its emphasis on diasporas, transnationalism, and comparative ethnic/racial studies, Global Asian Studies aims to better understand the globalized world, and redress some of the shortcomings of a limited focus on area (Asian studies) and ethnic studies (Asian American Studies) alone. [5] Anchored by an intersectional, social justice, and community-engaged framework, the pedagogical and intellectual work of Global Asian Studies encourages an examination of racial formations. [5] It also promotes an understanding of Asia and Asian diasporas as complex nexuses of knowledge and power, shaped and reshaped over time and space. [5] Students who want to minor in Global Asian Studies must complete 15 semester hours. [5]

Description: The minor in International Studies is multidisciplinary. Students can choose from offerings in three areas: World Markets and Development; Global Cultures and Societies; International Security and Governance. Students can choose to take course only in one area or across two or three of the areas. The minor requires 21 hours of courses that are international and comparative in content. In some cases, a course may count towards the International Studies minor and a students' major. Students should consult their advisor.

ProgramName: Bachelor of Fine Arts in Graphic Design
Department: College of Architecture, Design, and the Arts
Description: The Bachelor of Design in Graphic Design (BDes) is a pre-professional degree that prepares students for the rigors of designing for contemporary life. The curriculum is a synergy of research-informed strategic thinking and design methods, innovative making and aesthetics, and social and cultural awareness. Students learn to shape communication and interaction in a range of domains, from traditional print and web to mobile and emerging media. The program is centered on a core of required design classes, which becomes more specialized as students advance. The program culiminates with a senior capstone project where students work with a community partner to research and design a communication campaign that brings awareness to a topic of social importance.

Courses a focus on the civilizations of Ancient Greece and Rome, as well as the Ancient Near East, ancient Egypt, the Arabic world, and modern Greece—their languages, literatures, histories, philosophies, religions, arts, and archaeology. [3] Study in our program is inherently interdisciplinary and can touch upon many subjects, ranging from drama to astronomy, from mythology to geography, from science to gender studies, from philology to literary criticism, from political theory to sociology and anthropology—a complete liberal arts education in a single department. [3]

ProgramName: Bachelor of Science in Health Information Management
Requirements: Applicants to the Bachelor of Science in Health Information Management (BSHIM) Completion Program must have successfully completed 60 semester or 90 quarter total transferable undergraduate credit hours with a minimum cumulative GPA of 2.5 out of 4.0. Department: College of Applied Health Sciences
Description: If you're interested in healthcare and information technology, UIC's Bachelor of Science in health information management is perfect for you. Study topics like clinical diagnosis and procedure coding and reimbursement systems, data analysis, quality management and health information systems. After graduation, you're eligible to take the Registered Health Information Administrator (RHIA) exam. Available on campus or entirely online, our dynamic curriculum teaches you to properly manage and use information and information systems for healthcare planning, resource allocation and executive decision-making. Our award-winning faculty members have held prestigious roles in the healthcare industry, bringing expertise and real-world experience to our virtual and physical classrooms. Whether you’re on campus with us in Chicago or join our program online, you’ll gain the knowledge and experience you need to make a seamless transition to a career in the healthcare industry.
Accredidation: The Health Information Management program is accredited by the Commission on Accreditation for Health Informatics and Information Management Education (CAHIIM). Graduates from a CAHIIM accredited Bachelor of Science or Master of Science in HIM program are eligible to sit for the Registered Health Information Administrator (RHIA) certification exam. [11]

[2] The program includes a core curriculum that is supplemented with a focus area of coursework that you choose from a variety of fields based on your interests such as communities, social justice, early childhood, youth development and family studies. Description: The Bachelor of Science in Liberal Arts and Sciences, Major in Integrated Health Studies is a collaborative program of the College of Applied Health Sciences and the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences. [4] The program provides students the opportunity to explore the complexity of human health, from the level of the gene to society, by providing a diverse, interdisciplinary curriculum that includes core content spanning the life sciences, natural sciences, social sciences, and the humanities. [4] Students will graduate with a broad understanding of human structure and function in health and disease across the lifespan; a broad understanding of how human health and disease are impacted by culture, the environment, society, and personal behavior; and an appreciation for health issues that are unique to the urban environment and to the global society. [4] Upon completion of the bachelor's degree, graduates will be competitive for admission into professional and graduate health-related programs or entry into health-related careers. [4]

Requirements: To earn a Bachelor of Science in Liberal Arts and Sciences degree from UIC, students must complete university, college, and departmental degree requirements. Majors in Integrated Health Studies must complete either the Behavioral Health Concentration or the Health and Science Concentration. The major requires 38–52 semester hours, with no more than 22 hours at the 100 level and at least 6 semester hours at the 300 or 400 level. At least 19 hours of coursework for the major must be taken at UIC. [2, 5]

Description: The Bachelor of Science in Liberal Arts and Sciences, Major in Integrated Health Studies (IHS) is an innovative collaboration of the research and educational expertise in the health sciences across multiple programs, departments, and colleges at the University of Illinois at Chicago. The primary goal of the degree program is to offer a diverse, interdisciplinary curriculum in which students learn to integrate knowledge from the life sciences, natural sciences, social sciences and humanities, and apply it to their understanding of human health, disease, and health care. Students graduating with the Major in Integrated Health Studies in either the Behavioral Health Concentration or the Health and Science Concentration will have a comprehensive understanding of how human health and disease are impacted by culture, social and economic forces, the environment, and personal behavior, as well as an appreciation for health issues that are unique to rural, urban, and global contexts. [1]

Description: The program in Latin American and Latino Studies seeks to provide students with an understanding of the history, cultures, and contemporary issues of Latin Americans and Latinos in the U.S. using interdisciplinary approaches. [7] Courses for the major and minor cover Mexico, the Caribbean, and Central and South America as well as urbanization and social and political processes among Latino groups in Chicago and throughout the United States. [7] Comparative and diverse developmental perspectives illuminate linkages among the countries and peoples of the Americas. [7] A major or minor in Latin American and Latino Studies can serve as a useful basis for careers in public service, business, professional, or academic life related to Latin America or U.S. Latinos. [7] Requirements are designed so that students acquire exposure to both Latin American and Latino studies, with a general background from introductory-level courses and a more specialized study at the advanced level. [7] Students can tailor the remaining requirements toward a more general curriculum by taking an equal number of courses in Latin American Studies and in Latino Studies or pursue an area of specialization by taking more of their remaining courses in one of the two areas. [7] Students may also choose to take courses in a particular disciplinary area of the humanities (history and cultural studies) or the social sciences (anthropology, political science, sociology) or a combination of these areas. [7] Students are strongly encouraged to take at least one course on Mexico. [7]
Accredidation: The University of Illinois Chicago is accredited by the Higher Learning Commission. Description: UIC's minor in life science visualization empowers students who wish to complement a major area of study with concentrated study in science visualization for personal development and the expansion of career opportunities. As an interdisciplinary study, life science visualization has relevance to many disciplines including anthropology, art, biochemistry, bioengineering, biological sciences, chemistry, graphic design, integrated health studies, neuroscience, nursing, nutrition science and public health. [1] Those who can leverage both their knowledge and artistic skill to visualize science will have an advantage when presenting their research or seeking employment. Life science visualization is the important process of interpreting or translating science into visible form, and it is becoming a critical link in the bridge between information and knowledge in the 21st century. [1] Students who excel in visual problem-solving and value their curiosity in science can learn how to harness digital media technology to create dynamic works of art that advance understanding. Three-dimensional visualizations with interactive and motion media, virtual and augmented reality, educational games, as well as more traditional two-dimensional illustrations, are all being used today to communicate discovery and accelerate education in the life sciences. [1] The Minor in Life Science Visualization is designed for students in many disciplines who wish to enhance their understanding of visual thinking, education, and communication in the life sciences. [2, 5] Students declare an educational goal in a pre-health field to receive guidance from pre-health advisors on course selection and application materials for professional schools. [5]

[12] Students who desire to pursue careers for which a professional degree is required may take the necessary course work to apply to such programs in the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences. [13] Advisors encourage and support students in evaluating strengths and weaknesses, life goals, and their intended career path within individual appointments, small group sessions and workshops, as well as webinars. [12] Students will be guided in the incorporation of prerequisite coursework alongside bachelor's degree requirements to enhance their professional credentials and expand future career possibilities. [12]

Description: The goal of pre-law preparation at UIC is to give students the skills and information necessary to be able to enter an accredited law school after graduation. Law schools require a bachelor's degree prior to matriculation. Pre-law students must choose an undergraduate major and complete all requirements for that particular degree as there is no specific coursework required to apply to law school. The American Bar Association does stress that there are important skills, values, knowledge, and experience which students can acquire prior to law school and that will provide a sound foundation for a legal education.

[4] It provides the flexibility to complete prerequisite courses for various graduate and professional programs, including medical school, dentistry, pharmacy, and more. [4] The curriculum prepares future public health researchers and practitioners for careers in fields like environmental health, occupational health, and epidemiology. [4] To earn the degree, students must complete university and school requirements, which include prerequisite courses, general education, major courses in public health, and a selection of electives, totaling 120 hours. [3] In consultation with an advisor, students develop an area of focus by selecting 18 hours of courses from a list of bench, lab, and applied sciences. [3]

Description: In the Public Policy major at UIC, you’ll learn how to design, implement, and evaluate the policies that shape our world. Public policy is about more than government—it’s about solving problems, promoting fairness, and designing better systems for everyone. At UIC, you’ll explore how policy decisions are made, who influences them, and how to use evidence and analysis to improve public outcomes. [8] Through hands-on coursework and real-world case studies, you’ll develop skills that employers are looking for: data analysis, policy evaluation, critical thinking, persuasive writing, and effective communication. [8] Our alumni go on to careers in the public, private, and nonprofit sectors. Many continue their studies in graduate school. What they have in common is a vision for a better future and the expertise from UIC's Public Policy program to help build it. [8]

Description: The minor in public policy is designed to enhance student understanding of public problems and how governments attempt to address them. [3] Public policy affects all aspects of society from urban development to healthcare, the environment, education, international relations, and more. [3] A minor in public policy may be useful for students considering careers in a variety of policy-related fields, including jobs in policy analysis, research, public administration, nonprofit management, program evaluation, and as consultants for business and government entities. [3] Students pursuing a minor in Public Policy will deepen their understanding of public problems, policy solutions, and their own role as individual citizens in the policy environment. [3] Students can select electives to focus their minor on a substantive policy are of their choice (e.g. environmental policy, urban policy, crime and justice policy, etc.). [3] The minor in public policy would also be beneficial to students that plan to be employed in fields that are regulated by the government (engineering, technology, architecture, education, health care, sciences, and anyone who expects to play a leadership role in a business). [3] Employees in these roles need to understand how decisions are made and how nongovernmental actors (them) are able to shape these decisions. [3]

Requirements: To complete the Minor in Social Justice, students must take three core courses (SJ 101, SJ 201, and SJ 301) and two elective courses. The elective courses can be chosen from a range of departments within the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences. [4]

Description: Social justice is an interdisciplinary and growing field of study that critically explores issues and social movements focused on equality, fairness, and inclusion. The minor seeks to provide students with the breadth and depth of knowledge to achieve a critical understanding of justice, equality, and marginality, both in the United States and in the world at large. [4] The minor will be housed in the Department of Gender and Women's Studies, but is a collaboration of multiple departments within the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences. [4] Coursework examines the impact of racial and gender inequalities upon American society, examines social movements to redress such inequalities, and situates such struggles in relation to larger processes of empire, nation building, and globalization. [4]

Description: Sociology is the study of social life, including individuals, groups, organizations, institutions, and societies. [7] Sociologists investigate the social causes and consequences of human behavior and interaction, such as inequality, poverty, discrimination, and urbanization. [7] While offering a general sociology curriculum, the program particularly focuses on how social inequalities are structured and legislated, how they are supported by cultural representations and hegemonic ideologies, and how people navigate and push back against them in their everyday lives. [7] The program specializes in the study of: race, ethnicity, and immigration; gender and sexualities; organizations and the economy; politics, globalization, and social change; urban and spatial inequality; and health, science, and knowledge. [7] Students learn multiple methodological approaches for the study of social life, such as ethnography, in-depth interviews, survey research, focus groups, statistical analysis of secondary data, and the use of comparative historical methods. [7] Sociology majors in the program also explore how to actively use research-based evidence to increase the quality of life for the residents of Chicago, the state, the nation, and the world. [7] Sociology develops skills in analyzing, synthesizing, generalizing, and communicating data, information and knowledge. [7] Courses stress both logic and data analysis as well as careful and thoughtful reading, discussion, and writing. [7] Sociology's subject matter includes relationships among economic, political, cultural, and social factors and explores the impact of such forces on individuals and society. [7] This inclusive framework and general training lies at the heart of a liberal education for lifetime learning. [7] A major in sociology will prepare students to undertake graduate studies in sociology, and admission to other professional and graduate programs in medicine, health, law, urban planning, social work, education, and business. [7] It is also an excellent preparation for a wide variety of occupations in business and industry, the justice system, community and social services, government, education, social justice, and research. [7]

[2] Before graduating, each student is required to produce and document a final BFA thesis exhibition. [2] The School of Art & Art History prepares students to enrich and transform the world through their creativity and vision. [7] Students are encouraged to immerse themselves in an interdisciplinary program that explores the social, conceptual, and aesthetic possibilities of art. [7] Central to UIC's approach are studio courses with internationally renowned faculty that engage students in independent research and encourage the development of significant creative work. [7] Studio courses utilize an array of media, including drawing, painting, photography, moving image, new media arts, performance, and sculpture. [7] In addition to studio courses, students participate in seminars that interrogate the practice and theory of contemporary art. [7]

Description: UIC's four year Urban Studies program offers students the opportunity to study cities in order to transform cities once they graduate. [7] Our students experience and analyze urban issues from many different academic and practical perspectives in a department dedicated exclusively to the city. [7] The Urban Studies (formerly Urban and Public Affairs) degree is a pre-professional program that prepares students to enter urban professions and graduate programs. [7] Students will gain knowledge and understanding of the complexity and diversity of cities as well as seek specializations in particular issues affecting cities. [7] Aside from this, students have the opportunity to complete internships and to acquire computer, research, and other skills proper of the field of urban planning and policy. [7]

Requirements: First-year students interested in admission to the Bachelor of Arts in Urban Studies must complete a common application to the University and be admitted by the Department of Urban Planning and Policy, College of Urban Planning and Public Affairs. [3] Admission is competitive, and preference is given to those applicants selected to have the best potential for academic success. [3] Transfer students who have completed a minimum of 24 semester or 36 quarter hours of transferable college classroom credit may apply to transfer into the program. [3] The minimum transfer grade point average for admission is 2.5 on a 4.0 scale. [3]

Description: The Minor in Urban Studies provides students in many disciplines the opportunity to gain a further understanding of urban phenomena, the complex interactions between local and global forces, and the needs and opportunities of Chicago and other “Great Cities” historically, in the present and moving forward. [3] It is an 18-credit-hour interdisciplinary program focused on exploring cities and urban processes through an array of disciplinary lenses. [2] The program aims to prepare students to better understand the complex challenges of urbanization and the rapid pace of change in 21st-century cities, positioning them to effectively address these challenges as both professionals and citizens.
